query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an adaptive nanohierarchical heterostructure into the CoCrFeNi matrix via targeted alloying or surface treatment will enable the in‐situ formation of nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates that protect the friction interface, resulting in a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix that, in its untreated state, exhibits rising friction and wear issues—especially at high temperatures due to adhesive wear and oxidation.
generation.intervention: Implement an alloy modification or surface treatment designed to promote compositional segregation and controlled phase formation during wear, thereby forming an adaptive nanohierarchical heterostructure with embedded nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests conducted in ambient air at temperatures ranging from ~25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C, under moderate sliding loads (e.g., around 10 N) and realistic sliding distances, replicating typical wear environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a gradient nanostructured layer that at lower temperatures promotes multiple deformation pathways (via nano-coupled grains) to distribute stress, while at higher temperatures it facilitates tribochemical reactions to form a dense nanocrystalline oxide (glaze) layer that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the heterostructure releases frictional stress through adaptive plasticity provided by nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates, reducing localized strain. At elevated temperatures, the same structure accelerates the formation of a protective oxide glaze via tribo-oxidation, thereby mitigating adhesive and oxidative wear, and maintaining a low coefficient of friction over the full temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified sample is expected to exhibit a significantly lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range, maintaining performance at both room temperature and 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The original, unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which is prone to increased wear and friction—especially at higher temperatures due to softening, adhesion, and oxidation issues.
generation.boundary: The effect is specified for sliding conditions between room temperature and 800 °C under moderate loads (e.g., around 10 N) in ambient air. Extreme loads or aggressive environmental conditions outside these parameters may yield different results.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the friction and wear improvements is uncertain and likely depends on the uniformity and stability of the induced nanohierarchical heterostructure. Long-term durability and scale-up effects under variable sliding conditions also require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one set modified to induce the adaptive nanohierarchical heterostructure through controlled alloying/surface treatment, and a control set using the standard homogeneous alloy. Conduct sliding wear tests at both room temperature (≈25 °C) and 800 °C under identical loads (≈10 N) and sliding distances.
measurements: Real-time measurement of the coefficient of friction
Quantification of wear rate via mass loss or volumetric analysis
Surface and cross-sectional analysis (SEM, EDS, XRD) to identify the presence and characteristics of nano-coupled grains, nanoprecipitates, and oxide glaze layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified CoCrFeNi samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the control samples at both temperature extremes, or if the adaptive nanohierarchical and oxide glaze structures are not observed under high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

To summarize, this work proposes a paradigm for the development of ultra-wear-resistant alloys by combining A1 to A3 nano-coupled grains with A2 nanoprecipitates. The designed NiX is capable of activating favorable microstructure evolution and tribo-reaction during sliding, an effect that we refer to as adaptive friction interface protection. Contributing to the roles co-played by nanohierarchical architecture and spatial composition undulation, bulk NiX achieves ultralow wear rate between RT and 800 °C, which heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for any bulk alloys or composites. Such wear response found in the current CCA can be selectively applicable to other alloy systems to achieve pleasing wear resistance.

chosen.approach: Adaptive nanohierarchical heterostructure for friction interface protection
